title: What's the difference between deodorant and antiperspirant?
summary: Josh and Chuck explain the difference between deodorant and antiperspirant. Deodorant masks or kills odor-causing bacteria on the skin (often with triclosan and perfume) but does not stop sweating; antiperspirant uses aluminum and zirconium compounds to plug sweat glands and reduce sweat. Body odor comes from bacteria breaking down fats and proteins secreted by apocrine glands, not from sweat itself from eccrine glands. The hosts cover odor types, a Leakey predator-deterrent theory, the 1950s-60s advertising history (Arrid Extra Dry, Mad Men, the 1903 Everdry swab product), FDA regulation of both as over-the-counter drugs, aluminum health concerns (cancer, kidney disease warning label), market predictions tied to aging baby boomers, global warming, and bovine growth hormones, and a segment on HowStuffWorks homepage art for the article on ativism.

segments.title: Opening banter and body odor types
segments.summary: Hosts open with a joke about poker player Michael Wax being ejected from Borgata in Atlantic City for body odor, then discuss individual odor types, diet effects on odor, and a pregnancy odor study.

segments.title: Predator theory of smell
segments.summary: Chuck mentions a theory from anthropologist Leakey that human body odor evolved to ward off predators, noting it is less relevant today.

segments.title: Deodorant vs antiperspirant basics
segments.summary: The hosts establish that deodorant and antiperspirant are different: antiperspirant stops sweating, while deodorant only masks odor.

segments.title: Source of body odor: sweat glands and bacteria
segments.summary: Body odor comes from bacteria on the skin breaking down fats and proteins carried out by apocrine glands; eccrine glands secrete salt and water with no smell. Armpits are the main source of odor.

segments.title: History of deodorant and advertising
segments.summary: The hosts discuss the rise of deodorant in the 1950s in the US, the social taboo on smelling, the Mad Men show's depiction of antiperspirant ads, and the 1903 Ever Dry product that used a swab and was acidic.

segments.title: Market forecasts for deodorant sales
segments.summary: Chuck gives a sales figure of two point five billion dollars in 2006 and predicts market changes from aging baby boomers, hotter summers from global warming, and earlier puberty from bovine growth hormones.

segments.title: How each product works and aluminum concerns
segments.summary: Deodorants include bacteria-killing triclosan and perfume; antiperspirants plug sweat glands with aluminum and zirconium. Both are FDA-regulated over-the-counter drugs, and the hosts discuss cancer and kidney-related concerns about aluminum and a kidney warning label.

segments.title: Off-brand and natural deodorants
segments.summary: The hosts discuss the statistic that some Americans do not use deodorant or use off-brand products, and note natural brands such as Tom's of Maine have grown in the market.

segments.title: Sign-off and homepage art for ativism
segments.summary: Hosts plug the HowStuffWorks article on ativism, describe writer Katie Clambert's homepage art, and sign off with an email address for feedback.
